## Talk

### Slide 1 · Event-based Self-Checkout: Code Walkthrough · 0:20

Good evening. My name is Shilin. Today I show the code of my Assignment 6. In this version, the microservices communicate only through Kafka events. I use one story from the start to the end of the talk.

### Slide 2 · One story for the full talk · 0:40

I use one scenario for the full talk. Station 7 starts transaction tx-42. It scans 3 items. Then it completes the transaction. We follow these requests through the code. First, I show the architecture and the design decisions. Next, I start at the entry point and follow the checkout saga. Then I show the event bus, the error cases, and the popular-items window. At the end, I talk about the results, the challenges, and the future work.

### Slide 3 · Architecture and design · 0:05

Part one is the architecture and the design decisions.

### Slide 4 · What changed from Assignment 5 · 0:45

This slide shows the change from Assignment 5. In Assignment 5, services called each other over HTTP. Now, services communicate only through Kafka topics. A service does not know the address of another service. It knows only the topic names. If a service is down, its commands wait in Kafka. The request does not fail at once. The cost is at-least-once delivery. So every handler has to be idempotent. The load client, the public API, and the databases did not change.

### Slide 5 · Architecture · 1:15

This is the architecture. The client sends HTTP requests to the gateway on port 8080. The gateway only routes each request to the service that owns the path. It has no business logic, no database, and no broker connection. Next, there are four services. Each service has its own process and its own SQLite file. Payment is the orchestrator of the checkout saga. Below the services, there are six Kafka topics. Each topic has one partition, so the order of events is the order of production. Now the saga starts. Each pulse is one Kafka record. Payment sends a command, and the service sends a reply to payment. Then I show the two data feeds: the catalog feed and the scan feed. Last, the crate service-kit holds the shared code. It has the event bus and the SQLite connection code, but no domain types.

### Slide 6 · Event catalog · 0:45

This table is the event contract. Blue items are commands, and orange items are replies. Payment sends commands to basket and to inventory. Basket and inventory send replies to payment. The key is the transaction id or the saga id. That way, all messages for one saga stay in order. There are also two data feeds. The catalog topic is compacted, and basket reads the newest catalog at startup. The scan topic carries one event for each accepted scan. A rejection reply carries the same error code as before. So the client sees the same errors as in Assignment 5.

### Slide 7 · Key design decisions · 1:15

Here are the key decisions. First, checkout uses orchestration. Payment holds the saga state, so one place shows each step and each rollback. Second, scans use choreography. Analytics only listens to the scan topic. A new consumer, for example fraud detection, needs no change in basket. Third, basket uses a transactional outbox. The scan and its event commit in the same local transaction, so no event is lost. Fourth, the catalog is a compacted topic. Basket checks SKUs and prices locally, without a call to inventory. Fifth, delivery is at least once, and every handler is idempotent. Sixth, each topic has one partition, so the order is easy to verify. The trade-off is clear. Events give temporal decoupling and a durable log. But they add a broker to operate, and each hop adds latency.

### Slide 8 · Code walkthrough · 0:05

Part two is the code. I follow the completion of tx-42.

### Slide 9 · Entry point: from HTTP to payment-service · 0:50

Execution starts at the gateway. The gateway matches the path. The complete request goes to payment on port 8083. Any other path, for example an internal path, gets 404. Now look at the main function of payment. First, it opens its SQLite file and connects to Kafka. Bus connect also makes the six topics if they do not exist. Next, it runs recovery for all unfinished sagas. At startup, no request is in flight, so these sagas come from a previous run. Then it starts the consumer and a recovery timer. Last, it serves HTTP. At shutdown, it flushes both producers, so no queued record is lost.

### Slide 10 · Request-reply over events · 0:50

The client API is synchronous. The client waits for a receipt. But the saga is asynchronous. This function joins the two worlds. First, it writes the saga row with the state STARTED. Next, it puts a oneshot sender in a waiter map. The saga id is the correlation id. A drop guard removes the waiter when the request ends, in all cases. Then it publishes the Checkout command. Last, it waits for the outcome, for a maximum of ten seconds. The consumer task completes the waiter with a receipt or with an error. If the time ends first, the client gets 503, and recovery finishes the saga later.

### Slide 11 · The checkout saga · 0:40

This is the saga for tx-42. Every arrow between two services is one Kafka record. Payment sends Checkout, and basket locks the basket. Then payment sends Reserve, and inventory reserves all lines or none. If the stock is not sufficient, payment sends Release, and the client gets 409. If the stock is reserved, payment records the payment. This step is the pivot. After the pivot, the saga cannot go back. So the client gets the receipt right at the pivot. Basket completes a few milliseconds later.

### Slide 12 · Try it: saga state machine · 0:50

This simulator shows the same saga as a state machine. I select a scenario and step through it. In the happy path, the saga goes from STARTED to BASKET_LOCKED, then to STOCK_RESERVED, and then to COMPLETED. Look at the client column. The receipt comes at STOCK_RESERVED, not at COMPLETED. Now I select inventory down. The saga stops in BASKET_LOCKED. After the ten-second timeout, the client gets 503. Then recovery moves the saga to COMPENSATING and sends Cancel. When inventory is back, it applies Reserve and then Cancel, in order. Then the saga goes to RELEASING and to ABORTED. Last, I click redeliver. The same reply arrives again, and zero rows change.

### Slide 13 · State pattern with compare-and-set · 1:00

This is the core of payment. The pair of saga state and event type selects the next step. For example, STARTED plus BasketLocked moves the saga to BASKET_LOCKED and sends Reserve. BASKET_LOCKED plus StockReserved is the pivot. It records the payment, answers the client, and sends Complete. Every transition is a compare-and-set in SQL. The update has the expected state in its WHERE clause. If a reply is a duplicate, the state is already different. So the update changes zero rows, and payment sends no command. Any other pair is stale, and payment ignores it.

### Slide 14 · Event bus: ordered per key, parallel across keys · 1:10

All three consumers use this one function, bus run. The first version handled one record at a time. A command waited behind about 100 stations of scans. The second version keeps order only per key. It takes a slot from a semaphore, so a maximum of 64 records run at the same time. A new task with the same key waits for the previous task with that key. That way, the commands of one saga stay in order, and different keys run in parallel. The submitted version adds an acker task. The acker waits for each reply to reach Kafka. Only then does it store the offset, in topic order. If the service crashes before this point, Kafka delivers the record again. The function is a template. Each service gives only its handle function, as a strategy.

### Slide 15 · Error handling and edge cases · 1:10

The code has two classes of errors. A business refusal, for example insufficient stock, is final. The handler turns it into a rejection event, and the client gets the same 409 as before. An infrastructure failure, for example a database error, is temporary. The handler returns an error, and the bus tries the same record again. The table shows the edge cases. Duplicate commands return the same result. A Reserve that arrives after its Cancel finds a tombstone, so it cannot take stock. A scan that races a completion finds the basket in CHECKING_OUT and gets 409. If inventory is down, the client gets 503 after ten seconds. Recovery then sends Cancel. When inventory is back, the stock returns and the basket opens again. If basket is down after the pivot, the client still gets the receipt.

### Slide 16 · Popular items · 1 · From scan to analytics · 0:50

Let's go back to the scans of tx-42. They feed the popular-items window. All of this runs in one local transaction. Basket-service checks that the basket is open and looks up the SKU in its local catalog. It adds the line, bumps the total, and writes one outbox row. The outbox sequence has no gaps and follows the commit order, so it works as a global scan number. The client gets its answer right after the commit. Then a relay task publishes the outbox rows to the scan topic, in order. If a delivery fails, it goes back to the last confirmed sequence. After a restart, it picks up from the last sequence in the topic. On the other side, analytics reads the topic in batches of up to 5,000.

### Slide 17 · Popular items · 2 · Hopping window · 1:10

The window counts scans, not seconds. The defaults are a window size of 1000 and a slide of 500. The window end is the last sequence, rounded down to a multiple of the slide. The window start is the end minus the size, plus one. I move the slider. At sequence 1,499, the published window is still 1 to 1,000. At sequence 1,500, a boundary is crossed. Analytics publishes the window 501 to 1,500 and ranks the SKUs by count. Scans at or below the end minus the size are not necessary any more, so analytics deletes them. Now I inject a duplicate. The cursor skips it. Then I inject a gap. The batch stops at the gap and waits until the relay sends the lost event again.

### Slide 18 · Popular items · 3 · Persistence and reads · 0:50

This is the persistence of the window. One SQLite transaction does all the work. It skips duplicates and stops at a gap. It moves the cursor. If a boundary is crossed, it ranks the SKUs, saves the snapshot, and trims old scans. Because all of this commits together, a replay never counts a scan twice. The Kafka offset is stored only after this commit. For a read, analytics first reads the newest sequence in the topic. Then it waits until its cursor reaches that sequence. If Kafka is down, it serves the last snapshot.

### Slide 19 · Live demo: tx-42 through the gateway · 1:00

Now a live demo. The services and Kafka run on my laptop. The live transaction id is the next id in the database, not tx-42. I start a transaction for station 7 and scan three items. Each scan returns in a few milliseconds. Then I complete the transaction. The receipt comes back after the saga, in less than twenty milliseconds. The status can still show OPEN, because Complete arrives at basket a few milliseconds later. Next, I send 600 scans. The slide is 500, so the sequence crosses a window boundary. Now the popular items show a new window. On a fresh database, it is 1 to 500. The low-stock list includes the SKUs that the saga reserved. If the gateway is not available, the panel shows a recorded run of the same steps.

### Slide 20 · Reflections · 0:05

Part three is reflections.

### Slide 21 · Results: A1–A6 under the same load test · 0:45

This chart compares all six assignments under the same load test. It shows completed transactions per second. Each station waits for a response before it sends the next request. So every millisecond of wait cuts the throughput. At default load, A1 to A5 complete about 250 transactions per second. A6 completes 221, the lowest value. Four broker hops, that is two request-reply round trips, come before the pivot. Under stress, A6 completes 232 per second, the highest value. It also has the most scans: 7,239 per second. Group commit lets queued writes share one fsync. That means the basket SQLite writer is no longer the limit. But group commit is a configuration, not an architecture. A1 to A5 commit each write alone. With group commit, A5 reaches 304 per second under stress. All A6 runs passed the cross-database verifier.

### Slide 22 · Challenges and how I solved them · 1:25

I had five main challenges. First, the basket consumer stopped during one run. The Kafka 4.1 coordinator failed an offset fetch with an internal error. After that, librdkafka kept the partition but did not fetch from it. My fix was to rejoin the group after any consume error. I also upgraded the broker to 4.3.2. Second, completions took seconds under stress. Each consumer handled one record at a time, so a command waited behind many scans. Per-key concurrency fixed this. Third, each scan waited for Kafka. Now a scan returns after the outbox commit, and the relay publishes it right after. Fourth, the receipt waited for basket. Now payment answers at the pivot. Fifth, each saga hop waited for the producer to batch records. Now saga records go out at once, and only scans wait 5 milliseconds. The cost is clear. Analytics and the basket status can trail by a few milliseconds.

### Slide 23 · Future improvements · 1:00

If I had more time, I would make these changes. For robustness, I would add a dead-letter topic. Today, a poison record retries forever and blocks its key. I would also add a versioned schema, for example Avro with a schema registry. A real deployment needs a broker cluster with replication. A trace id equal to the saga id would help to find a stalled saga. For performance, I would add partitions to the command topics. The key stays the same, so the order per saga does not change. I would also run the broker outside the Docker Desktop VM. Today, each saga hop crosses this VM.

## Backup answers for Q&A

### Slide 25 · Backup · Why not Kafka exactly-once transactions?

Kafka transactions make a cycle atomic only inside Kafka. My handlers also write to SQLite. Kafka cannot put the SQLite commit in the same transaction. So a crash can still happen between the database commit and the offset commit. For this reason, I accept redelivery. Each handler is idempotent. Payment uses compare-and-set. Basket and inventory use tombstones. Analytics uses a sequence cursor.

### Slide 26 · Backup · Why one partition per topic?

One partition gives a total order for each topic. This order makes the design simple to verify. The consumer still handles up to 64 different keys at the same time. Under stress, the limit was the basket SQLite writer, not Kafka. Group commit removed this limit. More partitions are possible for the command topics. The key stays the transaction id or the saga id, so the order per key does not change. The scan topic must keep one partition, because the scan sequence is the clock of the window.

### Slide 27 · Backup · Why SQLite? Why a crash after the pivot is safe

Each service has one private SQLite file. WAL mode with full sync makes each commit durable. One writer per service makes the stock check and the decrement atomic. Queued writes share one fsync, up to 256 for each commit. Now, about a crash after the pivot. The saga row is STOCK_RESERVED, and the payment row exists. At restart, payment reads every unfinished saga. It sends Complete again. Basket applies it one time, and copies change nothing. Then the reply moves the saga to COMPLETED.
